passages.title: Redesigning a Small Flat
passages.text:
When Mai moved into her first flat, the rooms felt cold and empty. The bathroom had a cracked **tile** beside the bath, and the living room was covered with an ugly grey **carpet**. Her first job was to pull it up. Underneath she found a beautiful **wooden floor**, which only needed some polish to shine again.

Next, she turned to comfort. Daylight was too strong in the afternoon, so she hung white **blinds** that she could roll up or down. In the living room she bought **a big soft sofa**, perfect for watching films on rainy weekends, and she covered it with four colourful **sofa cushions**. One small **cushion** with a floral pattern became her favourite, and she often put it behind her back when she read a novel.

In the bedroom she chose a warm **duvet** for the winter months, because the flat gets chilly at night. "It doesn't look like a magazine photo," she says, "but it finally feels like home."

passages.title: A Busy Family Home
passages.text:
The Nguyen family lives in a three-storey house in Da Nang, and every room has a clear purpose. The two younger brothers **share a bedroom**, which they decorate with football posters. On weekdays the whole family is rarely together, but on Sundays they always **have dinner in the dining room** around a large wooden table.

Their father is a translator, so he likes to **work in the study** on the first floor, where it is quiet. Downstairs, the kitchen is the busiest place in the house. Beside the **kitchen sink** stands a shiny steel cabinet, and next to it there is **a fridge-freezer** that is big enough to store a week of food. The grey **floor tiles** are easy to clean, which is important with two active boys.

Their mother handles the laundry at the back of the house. "I **use the washing machine** every evening," she says, "otherwise the pile of sports clothes becomes impossible." Despite all the work, the family agrees that this house is exactly what they need.

passages.title: Learning to Cook at Fifty
passages.text:
At fifty, Hung decided to join a cooking class because he was tired of ready meals. "I want to become **a good cook**," he told the teacher. The first lesson was about meat and fish. The teacher explained that **veal** comes from young cows and is very tender, while **lamb** is the meat of young sheep and has a stronger flavour. For fish, she recommended **mackerel**, which is cheap, rich in oil and healthy.

Then came the methods. For beginners, the easiest way is to **boil** potatoes or eggs in a saucepan with plenty of water. Next, the students learned to **fry** onions in a frying pan until they turned golden. A piece of fish tastes wonderful if you **grill** it under a hot grill for just a few minutes. For Sunday lunch, you can **roast** a leg of lamb in the oven with oil and herbs, but if you prefer something sweet, **bake** a cake with flour, eggs and sugar instead.

By the end of the course, Hung was proud of his progress. His family, he says, has stopped ordering takeaway completely.

passages.title: A Weekend Walk
passages.text:
Last Saturday, Lan and her cousin took a trip to a small village near Hue. They knew they would **be short on time**, so they planned only a half-day walk and packed everything into one **rucksack**. They left at dawn, and the path led through some cool **woods**, where birds were singing in every tree.

After an hour they reached a wide open space **on the banks of the river**, and they sat down to rest and eat their sandwiches. The **scenery** was stunning: green hills, white clouds and little fishing boats floating slowly past. Lan took many photos, but her cousin slipped on the wet grass while trying to get a better view. When he stood up, he laughed loudly. "Look at me! I **have got** mud **on** my trousers!"

They walked back to the bus stop tired but happy, and they promised to return in the rainy season.

passages.title: Speaking Clearly in English
passages.text:
Many learners worry about how they sound when they speak English. In fact, you can **have a good accent** without sounding like a native speaker; what matters is clarity. The first step is to learn the **alphabet** properly, because each letter name contains a sound that you must produce correctly. English has about twenty **consonant** sounds, such as /p/, /t/ and /s/, and twelve pure **vowel** sounds, such as /i:/ and /æ/. Vietnamese speakers often leave out final consonants, so it is useful to record your voice and listen to it carefully.

Pronouncing each word **accurately** takes time, but speed can come later. Teachers say that learners who speak **fluently** are not always the most accurate, and that is perfectly normal. To **become more fluent**, read aloud for ten minutes every day and repeat short phrases until they feel natural.

Finally, remember that the real goal is to **make yourself understood**, not to be perfect. If the listener understands your message, you are already communicating successfully.

passages.title: Habits of Successful Learners
passages.text:
Teachers often notice that successful students share several habits. First, they **have a wide vocabulary**, so they can express ideas in many different ways. To **increase your vocabulary**, you can read news articles and keep a notebook of new words, reviewing it every week.

Second, you should **be willing to** speak even when you feel nervous, because silence never improves your English. Good learners also **experiment with** different study methods, such as flashcards, podcasts and word games, until they find the one that suits them.

It is normal to **get things wrong** at first, and clever students are not afraid of it. Remember to **learn from your mistakes** instead of feeling ashamed, and keep a list of the errors you often repeat. Over time, you will **make progress**, even if it feels slow today. Some children **pick things up** from cartoons without any effort, but adults usually need regular practice and patience.

passages.title: Why Some People Learn Faster
passages.text:
My friend Khoa seems to **have a good ear for language**; he can repeat a new sentence perfectly after hearing it only once. As a **language learner**, I used to feel jealous of him. But a recent talk by an experienced teacher helped me understand that talent is only a small part of the story.

"How well a student will **get on** depends mostly on daily habits," she said. Many students **have problems with** grammar or listening, and the solution is not to give up but to **develop an effective strategy**. For example, you can choose one skill, listening **in particular**, and work on it for a month. She suggested watching short videos with subtitles first, then without them, and writing down any phrases that sound useful.

I tried her plan for four weeks. It was not magic, but I understood more every week, and I stopped comparing myself with Khoa.

passages.title: A Gym Membership Story
passages.text:
My best friend Binh and I met on the first day of university, and **we've been mates ever since**. Last year, during exam season, we decided to **engage in** regular exercise to help us **get through** the stressful weeks. We joined a gym near campus, where the manager explained that our **current** membership rate was very cheap. However, we had to **agree not to withdraw** our deposit for twelve months.

We signed immediately because the price was so low. Every morning before lectures we ran on the machines or lifted light weights, and at night we slept much better than before. When the exams finally ended, we both felt stronger and calmer.

Now the end of the deal is close: the discount card will **run out** next month, so we must decide whether to renew it at the normal price. Honestly, we are leaning towards staying, because our daily workouts have become one of our favourite routines.
